connector: Hello, it’s Diana. I’m going to tea at Green Gables this afternoon, a proper invitation, and Mother says I’m to knock at the front door and not run into the kitchen the way I always do. I’ve got my second-best dress on. I’ve been practicing sitting with my toes together. Anne will do all the talking. She always does, and I don’t mind one bit.

guide2.label: Diana · before you open the book

transcripts.welcome: It’s Diana again. The question at the top is about an honest mistake turning into a real problem. I don’t know anything about that. All I know is I’m going to tea, and I’m awfully excited. So as you go, keep two lists in your head: what somebody meant to do, and what actually happened. Then there are doing words to sort, and a c-and-g rule that isn’t as simple as it looks.
transcripts.wgrd: Mother and I can watch the same thing and come away with two different stories. It used to make me cross. Now I think it’s just how people are. So when the box says pick one event, pick a small one, and put each person beside it. Then find the one thing somebody didn’t know. That’s usually the whole gap, right there. It was for Mother and me, anyway.
transcripts.dol: That’s my name in the bottom sentence without its capital letter, and Anne’s too. I mind that. The top one shows you how a sentence ends and starts again. The bottom one has two whole thoughts squashed together with nothing between them. Read it out loud and listen for the place your voice drops. That’s where the first thought wants a period and the next wants a capital letter.
transcripts.guide1: Four boxes. Word parts to type, then words to guess and match, then two sorts. I like sorts, because you can tell when you’re finished. Do them in order, and read every bit of a box before you tap anything, because two of them have a third column, and the third column is the tricky one. Anne would say the tricky one is the interesting one. Anne isn’t doing your sorting.
transcripts.morphology: Four little chunks for one job. I’d have said that was silly, four chunks that all mean not. But look at the letter right after each blank. That letter picks the chunk. Cover the blank, say what’s left, and try the chunk that sounds like it belongs on the front of it. The wrong one sounds wrong out loud. Anne says everything sounds better out loud, and for once she’s right.
transcripts.vocabulary: Three steps, then the flip cards, then a match. Here’s the thing about the flip cards. Guess first, out loud, before you tap. If you tap first there’s nothing to guess, and then the match is just remembering. In the match, do the two you’re surest of first. Then there are only two left and you can try them both ways and listen for which pair sounds right.
transcripts.grammar: Sorting doing words. Gertie Pye squeaks her pencil through every grammar lesson and it makes my blood run cold, so I’d rather do it here. Say each chip with its little word in front, the she or the they. Listen to the end of the doing word. Some change, some don’t, and some have a helper word stuck on the front. That’s your three groups. Name them in your own words.
transcripts.spelling: Two letters, and each one has two sounds. Say every word first, before you look at the columns, and listen for a hard sound or a soft one. Then look at the letter right after the c or the g. That letter decides it. Two of the words have both letters in them, one hard and one soft, so check those twice. Ruby Gillis would just guess. Don’t be Ruby.
transcripts.copia: One sentence, said three ways. Anne can say a thing six ways before she gets to the end of the lane, and I used to think that was showing off. It isn’t. It’s trying them on. Read the sentence, find the doing word, and change just that first. Then start it somewhere else. Then add where or how. Keep the one that sounds most like you.
transcripts.guide2: I’m dressed and I’m nervous, which is a silly thing to be about tea. The box on courage says it’s doing the hard thing while you’re still frightened. I’d have said courage was not being frightened. So while you read, watch for somebody who’s scared and goes anyway. And watch what fear looks like from the outside. Mostly it looks like standing very still.
transcripts.read: There are two stops, and I’ve read them, and I don’t like the sound of either one. One of them has my tea in it. The first stop asks whether somebody did anything wrong. Decide that before you read one more word, and then see if the rest of the chapter changes your mind. The second one asks the difference between a mistake and a wrong thing. Take your time on it.
transcripts.guide3: Well. Now you know. I was awfully sick, I had a headache all the next day, and Mother smelled my breath and that was that. She says Anne did it on purpose. I don’t believe it for one minute. Anne didn’t have any herself, she said she didn’t want any after the apples. But nobody’s asking me. They’re asking you, so show it from the book, not from how you feel.
transcripts.chapter: The first question is about what I drank, and why Anne didn’t know. Look at what Anne said when she set it down in front of me. The second is about Mother, and she’s my mother, so I’m not the one to ask. Put what she believes happened next to what happened. The third is about Marilla, and I wasn’t there. The hint gives you two things she did. Use both.
transcripts.wordconn: Your word-parts answer is saved. You made a word that means not something. Well, the whole afternoon was a not. Anne did not mean it. Mother does not believe her. I wasn’t even home to say goodbye. Look back at the word you chose and ask which person in the chapter it fits best. If it fits somebody, put them in your sentence. If it doesn’t, pick a different word.
transcripts.workshop: Sam wrote about the weather first, and then crossed it out. Anne’s chapter starts with October, a whole page of it, and I love October, but the story starts when Marilla says I can come to tea. So write your two first sentences, two different kinds, and read each one out loud. The one that makes you want to know what happens next is the one you star.

a.raw: anne carries the bottle to the sitting room she pours diana a drink
a.fixed: Anne carries the bottle to the sitting room. She pours Diana a drink.
a.why: Capital letters on the names Anne and Diana, a period to close the first thought, a capital S to start the next sentence, and a period at the end.

b.raw: diana knocked at the front door anne opened it in her second best
b.fixed: Diana knocked at the front door. Anne opened it in her second best.
b.why: The same pattern: capitals on the names Diana and Anne, a period where the first thought ends, a capital A to start the next sentence, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say whether the mistake was Anne’s, Marilla’s, or nobody’s, with one detail to back it up.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say what Mrs. Barry would have needed to know to change her mind.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say which of the two things Marilla did tells you more, and why.

fill1.h1: The root starts with the letter l. Which of the four chunks likes to sit in front of an l?
fill1.why: Before a root that starts with l, the “not” chunk is spelled with an l too: il + legal.

fill2.h1: The root starts with r. One of the four chunks is made for r.
fill2.why: Before a root that starts with r, the “not” chunk is spelled with an r: ir + regular.

fill3.h1: The root starts with p. Say “in-possible” out loud and feel how your lips want to close. Which chunk is spelled the way your mouth wants?
fill3.why: Before b, m or p, the “not” chunk is spelled with an m: im + possible.

fill4.h1: The root starts with c. That is not l, not r, not b, m or p. Which chunk is the ordinary one?
fill4.why: Before most letters, the “not” chunk is the plain one: in + correct.

match.cordial: Cordial has cor inside it, the Latin word for heart. Look for the meaning about being warm-hearted.
match.relent: Relent is what a hard person does when they finally soften. Look for the meaning about changing your mind.
match.incapable: Incapable starts with the “not” chunk and has capable inside it. Look for the meaning about not being able.
match.inexorable: Inexorable also starts with the “not” chunk, and the rest means “able to be begged.” Look for the meaning about refusing to give in.

sort.they walk: Say it with its little word: they walk. Nothing added at the end. Which group is the plain one?
sort.she walks: Say it: she walks. Listen to the end of the doing word. Something got added. Which group is that?
sort.she is walking: There is a helper word in front, and the doing word ends in a way that means it is happening right now. Which group has helpers?
sort.we hope: Say it: we hope. Nothing added at the end. Which group is the plain one?
sort.he hopes: Say it: he hopes. Listen to the very end of the doing word. Which group is for that ending?
sort.he is hoping: A helper word, then a doing word that is going on right now. Which group has helpers?
sort.cordial: Say it: COR-dial. The c is hard, and there is no soft sound anywhere in it. Which column is for hard only?
sort.cellar: Say it: SELL-ar. That c sounds like s. Look at the letter right after it. Which column is for soft?
sort.courage: Say it: CUR-idge. The c is hard, but listen to the g at the end. Two different sounds in one word. Which column is that?
sort.golden: Say it: GOLD-en. The g is hard, and nothing in it is soft. Which column is for hard only?
sort.genius: Say it: JEE-nyus. That g sounds like j. Look at the letter after it. Which column is for soft?
sort.gorgeous: Say it: GOR-jus. The first g is hard and the second one is soft. Two sounds, one word. Which column is that?
